title: "Dynamic Programming"
description: "Learn Dynamic Programming with a complete numerical recurrence, proof, counterexample and small tested implementation."
---

## One problem you can understand by hand

**LeetCode 198 — House Robber.** You have houses with values [2,7,9,3,1]. You cannot take two neighbouring houses. A greedy choice of the largest immediately visible house can block a better combination later.

A good algorithm explanation begins with the decision you need to make, not the method's name. Write down the smallest example and the exact choice available at each step.

## The approach that looks convincing but fails

Enumerate all subsets of houses and discard adjacent selections. There are up to 2^n subset choices, even though the outcome depends only on the last couple of positions.

Do not improve the code yet. Ask whether the information you need is already present in a smaller version of the same problem.

## The key reasoning step

Define a state by the FIRST i houses rather than by the exact list of already chosen houses. Any optimal answer either skips house i or takes it. Those cases are exhaustive and do not overlap.

## From actual numbers to mathematics

$$
DP[i]=\max(DP[i-1],DP[i-2]+a_i)
$$

**What every symbol means:** DP[i] is the maximum money obtainable from houses 1 through i; a_i is the money at house i. DP[i−1] means skip house i; DP[i−2]+a_i means take i and therefore skip its neighbour. Base cases: DP[0]=0 and DP[−1]=0 in this 1-based description.

**Now substitute numbers into that same relationship:** For houses [2,7,9,3,1]: DP[1]=max(0,0+2)=2; DP[2]=max(2,0+7)=7; DP[3]=max(7,2+9)=11; DP[4]=max(11,7+3)=11; DP[5]=max(11,11+1)=12. The best total is 12 (2+9+1).

If a recurrence contains two alternatives, identify which real-world decision each alternative represents. If the formula uses a maximum, say what is being maximised and why the alternatives cover all legal choices.

## Why the result is actually correct

Assume smaller prefixes have optimal stored results. Every feasible solution for i either includes i (forcing exclusion of i−1) or excludes i; taking the larger of both optimal subcases is therefore optimal.

A complete proof needs an initial state/base case, preservation of the hypothesis and an explanation that no valid possibility has been missed.

## Actual implementation

The [original, tested JavaScript implementation](../examples/patterns.mjs) exports `houseRobber`:

~~~js
import { houseRobber } from '../examples/patterns.mjs';

console.log(houseRobber([2,7,9,3,1]));
~~~

Run this from a `.mjs` file inside this topic directory. The same function is exercised by [the unit tests](../examples/patterns.test.mjs). The implementation is intentionally tiny so the recurrence remains visible.

## Complexity and failure conditions

**Cost model:** O(n) time because each house is processed once; O(1) extra space after storing only the previous two states. n is number of houses.

**A classic mistake:** Greedy 'always take the largest remaining house' does not correctly preserve adjacency constraints; DP solves a global choice using local reusable subproblems. If the houses form a circle (LC 213), the first and last cannot both be selected, so use two linear cases.

In interviews, identifying **why a tempting shortcut fails** is more valuable than memorising one template. For example, a greedy choice needs an exchange proof; if no such proof exists, dynamic programming may be necessary.

## Try teaching it back

Use only the numbers in the worked example and explain the state, choices, update, stopping condition, and why no better answer is excluded. Then change one assumption and explain what changes.
